item.title: Research Intern (Summer 2027)
item.description:
CNA is hiring a Research Intern for Summer 2027 at its Arlington, Virginia location. Interns are embedded in real study teams and either take on a self-contained research project or support multiple ongoing studies, applying rigorous analysis to real-world defense and security challenges. The role offers hands-on experience, mentorship, and networking opportunities in a collaborative, mission-driven environment.
Key responsibilities: Assist in defining and structuring analytical problems. Develop sound analytical techniques. Carry out analyses to logical conclusions. Communicate results both in writing and orally. Collaborate with expert researchers and analysts on complex national security issues. Contribute to projects that inform defense policy and operations. Present findings and insights to internal teams and potentially external stakeholders. Perform other duties as assigned.
Qualifications: A bachelor's degree in the physical sciences, engineering, operations research, mathematics, statistics, economics, international relations, or a related discipline. Applicants must be enrolled in a graduate program (master's or PhD) and have a strong interest in policy research, national defense, or security studies. Undergraduate research experience, including literature searches, analyses, and report writing, is required, and graduate-level coursework and experience are preferred. Required skills include experience with database manipulation and Microsoft Office (Word, Excel, PowerPoint), good interpersonal and oral and written communication, critical thinking, and organizational skills. Applicants must be able to obtain and maintain a security clearance, and U.S. citizenship is required.
Application and logistics: Apply by November 30, 2026. Preference is given to candidates who upload a resume, a cover letter describing their experience and why they want to intern with CNA, and transcripts (unofficial copies are accepted). The position is eligible for telecommuting or hybrid work at the supervisor's discretion, and interns may be required to work at CNA headquarters or other locations. All applicants are subject to a background investigation.

item.company: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
item.title: 2026 CDC Public Health Fellowships
item.description:
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) supports education, training and development across the public health workforce, including postgraduate experiential service-learning fellowships. Its Public Health Fellowships prepare fellows to protect the nation's health, filling workforce gaps in epidemiology, policy, economic analysis, data science, laboratory science, public health service delivery and more. Three fellowships are currently accepting applications, and most are based in Atlanta, GA. This listing was published by ProFellow on behalf of CDC.
The fellowships: (1) Public Health Informatics Fellowship Program: paid 2-year applied training for doctoral- or master's-prepared professionals, applying computer science, data analytics and data science to public health needs. (2) Steven M. Teutsch Prevention Effectiveness (PE) Fellowship: a paid 2-year postdoctoral research fellowship in quantitative policy analysis, health economics-based inquiry and integrative health services research, assessing the effectiveness, quality and cost of public health policies, programs and practices. (3) Evaluation Fellowship Program: a paid 2-year fellowship for master's and doctoral recipients in which fellows build evaluation skills while helping their host program build, expand or improve its evaluation activities.
Qualifications: These are postgraduate programs. Informatics requires a doctoral or master's degree, the Prevention Effectiveness Fellowship is postdoctoral, and the Evaluation Fellowship is for master's and doctoral recipients. Each fellowship has its own detailed eligibility requirements, which are on CDC's fellowships webpage and not in this listing.
Compensation and benefits: Salary depends on the fellow's degree (master's or doctorate), with a posted range of $84,238 to $100,964. Benefits include health, vision and dental coverage, retirement benefits, and annual and sick leave.
Deadlines: Public Health Informatics Fellowship Program: applications are open through November 6, 2026. Prevention Effectiveness Fellowship: open through January 8, 2027. Evaluation Fellowship Program: opens October 26, 2026 and closes January 7, 2027. Application components vary by fellowship; see CDC's Public Health Fellowships website for details.

item.company: Bureau of Indian Affairs (U.S. Department of the Interior)
item.title: Student Trainee (Administration and Office Support)
item.description:
The Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA), part of the U.S. Department of the Interior, is hiring Pathways interns, also called Student Trainees, who fill a wide variety of roles and functions in the offices and programs to which they are assigned. This is an open continuous announcement: applications are accepted and reviewed every two weeks until the posted closing date of January 29, 2027 (the announcement opened July 31, 2026). Interns learn about the nation-to-nation relationship between the federal government and federally recognized Tribal Nations and how BIA and Tribal Nations work together to oversee, protect, manage and use Indian Trust Lands and restricted lands.
Key responsibilities and training: Receive formal and on-the-job training to develop the knowledge and skills needed for entry-level positions within BIA. Education requirements under the GS-0399 Administration and Office Support Student Trainee standard are: GS-2, completion of high school or a GED; GS-3, one academic year of post-high school study; GS-4, two academic years of post-high school study or an associate's degree. Applicants must be students accepted for enrollment or enrolled and seeking a degree, diploma or certificate at a qualifying educational institution on a full- or half-time basis. Certificate programs must be at least one year of full-time post-secondary study. Students without a transcript, such as first-year or returning students, can submit a degree plan or other proof of enrollment, such as a course schedule, registration record, advisor-approved degree checklist or acceptance letter on official letterhead. All qualification requirements must be met by the closing date.
Conditions of employment: A one-year probationary period or two-year trial period applies. A background security investigation is required. Males born after 12/31/1959 must be registered with Selective Service. The incumbent may need to operate a government vehicle, which requires a valid driver's license and a safe driving record for the past four years.

item.title: Pickering, Rangel and Payne Fellowships (2027 Cycle)
item.description:
The U.S. Department of State is reestablishing the Thomas R. Pickering, Charles B. Rangel and Donald M. Payne Fellowships to streamline and unify these statutorily mandated Foreign Service recruitment and onboarding pathways. Through graduate education, professional development, mentorship, and domestic and overseas internships, the initiative aims to identify exceptional American talent and prepare a cadre of Foreign Service Officers. Fellows must complete a two-year master's degree program at a Department-approved university in the Washington, DC area and commit to a five-year service agreement with the Department after completing the fellowship and meeting entry requirements.
What the fellowship includes: graduate education, professional development, mentorship, a cohort experience in Washington, DC, and domestic and overseas internships, with updated academic support and financial assistance for the 2027 cycle. The posting does not list specific dollar amounts.
Eligibility: Applicants must be U.S. citizens with an undergraduate degree who are seeking admission to a two-year master's program in international affairs, public policy, development or a related field at an approved institution. A cumulative undergraduate GPA of 3.2 or higher on a 4.0 scale is required at application, and the bachelor's degree must be completed before the fellowship begins. Applicants must be prepared to obtain and maintain Department of State medical, security and suitability clearances. For the 2027 cycle only, conditional offers will be made pending successful completion of the Foreign Service Officer Test (FSOT) and the written exercise of the Foreign Service Officer Assessment (FSOA).
Estimated 2027 timeline (from the posting): FSOT registration runs September 10 to October 30, 2026 and December 31, 2026 to February 5, 2027. The FSOT testing windows are October 10 to 31, 2026 and January 30 to February 6, 2027, and applicants must take the FSOT in one of those windows to meet the application deadline. The application period is December 2026 to January 2027. Candidates are notified in March 2027, finalist interviews are held in Washington, DC in March 2027, offers go out in April 2027, orientation is in June 2027, and the two-year graduate program begins in fall 2027. The Payne Fellowship application details were still forthcoming at the time of the posting.

item.title: Summer Internship Program (SIP)
item.description:
The NIH Summer Internship Program (SIP) is a full-time, in-person summer research internship in the NIH Intramural Research Program (IRP). It is for community college, college, graduate and professional students who want to explore careers in research and healthcare. Interns work in a research group led by a Principal Investigator (PI) at one of the NIH Institutes and Centers. Research groups are located on all NIH campuses, including the main campus in Bethesda, Maryland. Opportunities span the biomedical, behavioral and social sciences and include basic, translational and clinical research. Interns may not work in administrative offices or outside the IRP.
What interns do and receive: Perform research in a PI's group. Take part in professional development programs focused on core competencies for healthcare, research and other science careers, educational and career programming, and a well-being and resilience program. Attend the Graduate and Professional School Fair in July and present research at Summer Poster Day in early August.
Qualifications: Applicants must be U.S. citizens or permanent residents; permanent residents must be attending, or have been accepted into, U.S. educational institutions. Applicants must be 18 by September 30, 2027 (graduating high school seniors who turn 18 by then may qualify if they live within 40 miles of an NIH campus). Applicants must be enrolled at least half-time in an accredited community college, college, university, graduate or professional program at the time of application, or be accepted into an accredited graduate program for the fall. Students interested in biology, engineering, epidemiology, psychology, mathematics, chemistry, pharmaceutical sciences, nursing, physics, computer science, bioinformatics and other health-related fields are invited to apply. Applicants with a family member working at NIH should note the strict nepotism policy, which may limit placement options.
Compensation and logistics: The internship must be completed between May 10 and August 31, 2027, with start and end dates set in consultation with the selecting PI. It is a full-time, in-person commitment; remote and virtual internships are not permitted, and interns must be available for the entire period, with no vacations or summer classes. Stipends are set annually by educational level; the posting does not give amounts. Free parking is available on each campus, NIH does not provide housing, and interns must show proof of health insurance.
How to apply: Apply through the NIH Application Center with a coursework list, CV or resume, a personal statement, and two references. The application closes Tuesday, January 26, 2027 at 12 pm ET, and reference letters are due Tuesday, February 2, 2027 at 12 pm ET. There is no centralized selection: individual PIs review applications and choose their own interns, so applicants should also contact PIs directly. Selection is completed by April 1. An application webinar is scheduled for November 17, 2026, 4 to 5 pm ET (virtual).

item.title: Consulting Intern, Government Procurement and Contracting Analyst
item.description:
This position was posted with no close date and applications may be reviewed or closed on a rolling basis — interested applicants should apply ASAP! The posting will be removed from Batten Connect on 11/11/2026.
BerryDunn's Local Government Practice Group serves clients running cities, towns, counties and school districts across the country. A core service is software system planning, including developing competitive request for proposal (RFP) documents that help clients evaluate large-scale software to replace legacy products, such as enterprise resource planning (ERP), permitting and land management, utility billing, electronic health records, and CAD/RMS and related public safety systems. As a Consulting Intern serving as a Government Procurement and Contracting Analyst, you receive guidance from the supervisors, consultants or principals leading each engagement and work mainly alongside a Manager who supports procurement planning across multiple project teams. The internship is based in BerryDunn's Portland, Maine office and runs from May 25, 2027 through August 6, 2027. The firm expects flexibility, a willingness to seek advice and a passion for learning.
Key responsibilities: Develop an understanding of the consulting process in local government. Assist with consulting engagements of all sizes. Support project management tasks such as tracking and reporting progress, conducting research, maintaining the project document repository and reviewing deliverables for quality assurance. Help prepare solicitation documents, including RFPs, scoring tools and templates. Follow appropriate diagnostic, data collection, fact-finding and data analysis practices. Keep supervisors informed of project status. Provide ad hoc assessments and briefings in response to client requests. Take part in team meetings and training and work as a team player on multiple client projects.
Qualifications: Currently enrolled in a BA, BS or MS program in political science, business administration, or public policy or administration, or hold an undergraduate degree in a relevant field and have at least 12 months of government procurement experience. Legal authorization to work in the U.S. without employer sponsorship, now or in the future. Strong organizational skills with the ability to manage multiple tasks and deadlines. Strong Microsoft Office skills and attention to detail. Demonstrated relationship-building experience and excellent writing and communication skills. Relevant experience in government, procurement or public administration is a plus. Willingness and ability to travel.
Compensation and application: The pay is $30 per hour. Applicants submit a resume and an unofficial transcript. The posting does not state an application deadline.

item.company: Asian Pacific American Institute for Congressional Studies (APAICS)
item.title: APAICS Summer Congressional Internship
item.description:
The APAICS Summer Congressional Internship is a paid, eight-week program for undergraduate students and eligible recent graduates interested in gaining experience in public policy and public service. Interns are placed in congressional offices in Washington, DC, where they gain hands-on experience in the legislative process while building leadership and professional skills. Interns also take part in APAICS programming designed to encourage political engagement, strengthen professional skills and foster an interest in public service careers.
Program expectations: Interns work 30 to 40 hours per week in their congressional host office, depending on the office's needs. They must attend orientation before the program starts, take part in APAICS events and weekly professional development sessions, and complete program reflections and evaluations.
Benefits: A $2,550 grant. Shared, furnished, dorm-style housing in Washington, DC (interns typically bring their own bedding, toiletries and kitchen supplies). A $200 Metro stipend. Domestic round-trip transportation to and from Washington, DC at the start and end of the internship.
Dates and location: The 2027 summer program runs June 7 to July 30, 2027, with orientation on June 2 and 3, 2027. The program is on site in Washington, DC.
How to apply: The application deadline is December 18, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. Do not apply through Handshake; applications submitted there will not be considered. Apply through the APAICS application portal at https://apaics.fillout.com/internship-summer-application. A complete application includes a one-page cover letter, a one-page resume, an academic transcript (unofficial is accepted), one letter of recommendation, and responses to three questions of no more than one page each, double-spaced: why you should be selected, how you have incorporated public service and will in your career, and a challenging situation you experienced and what you learned. Questions can go to programs@apaics.org.

item.company: ACMER Foundation (American Committee for Middle East Rights Foundation)
item.title: Leadership Development Program (LDP) Summer 2027 Internship
item.description:
The American Committee for Middle East Rights (ACMER) Foundation Leadership Development Program (LDP) Summer 2027 Internship is a paid internship for undergraduate students and young professionals interested in foreign policy and human rights issues. Interns are placed in congressional offices to gain direct insight into the policymaking processes that drive U.S. foreign policy, and they take part in a mandatory professional development and networking program. ACMER strongly encourages applications from people of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) descent and from anyone with a demonstrated interest in MENA-related foreign policy, human rights and national security. The program welcomes applicants from all backgrounds.
Program objectives: Promote MENA-American representation in legislative and advocacy processes and encourage engagement with MENA-related issues. Provide substantive, hands-on experience in congressional offices. Strengthen leadership skills and professional networks through structured programming and networking events.
Eligibility: U.S. citizenship is required. Candidates should ideally be pursuing degrees in international affairs, political science, law or a related field, with a minimum GPA of 3.0 on a 4.0 scale. Preference may be given to applicants who live in or attend school within the districts of participating congressional offices.
Program details: The program runs May to August 2027, with exact dates flexible, and full-time schedules are prioritized. The stipend is $5,000 paid by ACMER Foundation, and need-based additional financial assistance may be available. The program is in Washington, DC, interns arrange their own housing and must live in DC for the whole program, and virtual options are not available.
How to apply: Submit four short-answer questions, a PDF resume of two pages at most, a list of two to three references and an unofficial transcript through the application form. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis with a priority deadline of December 1, 2026 at 11:59 PM PT, and the application stays open after that date. Apply only through the application form, not LinkedIn or other job sites. An information session is on November 17 from 5 to 6 PM ET on Zoom. Interviews begin in December, host placement interviews continue through the fall, and a virtual orientation is held in the spring.

Strong analytical, problem-solving, written communication and presentation skills. item.company: Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), Executive Office of the President
item.title: ONDCP Unpaid Student Internship (Spring 2027)
item.description:
The Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), part of the Executive Office of the President, leads and coordinates the nation's drug policy so that it improves the health and lives of the American people. ONDCP develops and implements the National Drug Control Strategy and Budget. This is an unpaid internship in Washington, DC for the Spring 2027 term, which runs from January 19 to May 21, 2027.
Offices accepting interns: Applicants choose one office. The Office of the Director oversees policy development, implementation and coordination. The Office of Addiction Prevention supports federal policy on drug use prevention, early intervention, treatment and recovery. The Office of Grants and Programs manages ONDCP programs, including the High-Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas and Drug-Free Communities programs. The Office of External and Legislative Affairs handles relations with the media, Congress, state, local and Tribal governments and the public. The Office of Management and Administration handles human resources, facilities, procurement, security, IT and the internal budget. The Office of Performance and Budget coordinates budget requests and produces the National Drug Control Assessment. The Office of Supply Elimination develops international supply reduction efforts and coordinates interdiction. The Office of General Counsel provides legal services. The Office of Data and Research coordinates data and research that inform policy.
Eligibility: U.S. citizenship. At least 18 years old. Males must be registered with Selective Service. A commitment of at least 15 hours per week. Availability all day on Tuesday, January 19, 2027 for onboarding, and for the entire session, January 19 through May 21, 2027. Current enrollment, or enrollment to start a program within 5 months of graduation, at least half-time in an accredited undergraduate or graduate college, community college or university. item.title: Summer Associate Program (Summer 2027)
item.description:
RAND is a nonprofit, nonpartisan research organization focused on improving policy and decision making through high-quality research and objective analysis. Its Summer Associate Program introduces outstanding graduate students across the social, behavioral, policy and technical sciences to RAND, which researches a wide range of domestic and international social policy issues and national security problems. Summer Associates typically work for 12 weeks (60 work days) and are paid bi-weekly. They conduct research that can be completed during the assignment and present the results to the RAND community in a 15 to 30 minute briefing at the end, are closely mentored by one or two established RAND researchers, are encouraged to network beyond their mentorship team, and are invited to seminars within and outside RAND.
Work model and location: The summer 2027 program is hybrid, with in-person work at one of RAND's four U.S. offices (Santa Monica, CA; Washington, DC; Pittsburgh, PA; and Boston, MA) with remote flexibility, or fully remote from where you live. Office placement depends on the availability of in-person mentorship. Students must live in the U.S. throughout the assignment, excluding U.S. territories. International students who will live in the U.S. in summer 2027 are eligible.
Who is eligible: The program is designed for full-time doctoral students who have completed at least two years of graduate work and are within two years of finishing their doctorate. Master's students are eligible only in Engineering, Computer or Information Science, and Operations Research, and must graduate in December 2027 or later. The program does not hire high school students, undergraduates or postdoctoral fellows, and graduate students who will graduate before the summer are not eligible.
Qualifications: A keen interest in applied, policy-oriented research. Excellent analytic skills and proven ability in quantitative or qualitative research methods. Clear communication in English, verbal and written. The ability to work on a multidisciplinary team and a commitment to RAND's core values of quality and objectivity. Proof of the legal right to work in the U.S. on hire. U.S. citizenship is not required except for project work that needs it, and many national security and defense projects require eligibility for a U.S. security clearance. RAND seeks training in political science and history, engineering, computer and data science, international relations and security studies, biology and life sciences, industrial-organizational psychology, operations research, economics, health policy and public health, and education policy; positions are not available in every discipline or research area, and RAND does not know in advance which projects will need summer associates.
Compensation and how to apply: $32.00 per hour, overtime eligible. Applicants submit a resume or CV and a cover letter, answer three short questions online (substantive interests and experience, skills and methods, and why RAND and how the experience fits their career), and give contact details for two people who may later write recommendation letters, typically requested in late January or early February. Submit only one application. All applications are due by December 1, 2026. Interviews begin in late January and continue into February and March, and offers are typically extended in late March.

item.company: GovAI (Centre for the Governance of AI)
item.title: DC Summer Fellowship 2027
item.description:
The DC Summer Fellowship is a three-month, bipartisan opportunity run by GovAI to accelerate or launch careers in American AI governance and policy. Fellows spend June 7 to August 27, 2027 in Washington, DC, deepen their understanding of the field, connect with a network of experts and build their skills while conducting a research project of their choice under expert guidance. The program emphasizes bipartisan engagement, rigorous analysis and practical policy relevance, with a focus on how AI policy is shaped within the US political system. GovAI was founded at Yale University in 2016, now operates independently as a 501(c)(3) think tank, and aims to help decision-makers navigate the transition to a world with advanced AI.
What fellows do: Each fellow is paired with a supervisor from the GovAI team or network. Fellows spend the first two weeks exploring the AI policy landscape, then settle on a research proposal with their supervisors' input. The research could become a report, white paper, journal article, op-ed or blog post aimed at an AI policy audience. Alongside weekly supervisor meetings, fellows join Q&A sessions with AI policy experts, hands-on workshops and seminars, work-in-progress meetings for peer feedback, and social events, and they discuss follow-on career opportunities with GovAI's team and network.
Who should apply: The program welcomes early-career people entering US AI policy and experienced professionals moving into emerging tech policy from adjacent fields, including candidates from government, academia, industry and civil society. It is especially interested in relevant professional or research experience or graduate study in areas such as public policy, political science, engineering, computer science, economics, biosecurity, cybersecurity, China studies and risk management. There are no specific requirements or strict degree requirements, and promising undergraduates are welcome. Reviewers look for quality of work (clear, insightful, even-handed writing and reasoning), relevant expertise, judgment and team fit. Only candidates with the right to work in the U.S. may apply, and GovAI does not sponsor visas.
Stipend and logistics: Fellows receive a $24,500 stipend plus support for travel to DC, weekday lunches and a desk in GovAI's DC office. The role is in person and intended to be full-time. item.title: Hudson Institute Political Studies Summer Fellowship
item.description:
Hudson Institute Political Studies offers a fellowship in political theory and practice to college students and recent graduates, broadening and deepening their understanding of public policy and American political principles. The core of the program is a six-week summer program based in Washington, DC. For 2027 it runs in two sessions: Session I from May 24 to July 5 and Session II from June 28 to August 7. Admitted applicants are placed in one of the two sessions, and anyone who cannot attend a session can email Ayla McBreen at amcbreen@hudson.org to say which one and why.
What the program includes: (1) Rigorous seminars led by master teachers on week-long topics in political theory and public policy, with three hours of discussion every weekday morning after careful reading of classic texts and policy analyses. (2) Weekly policy workshops led by think tank experts and experienced government officials, where students engage in the policymaking process and work through policy problems. (3) A distinguished speaker series three afternoons per week, with national leaders from government, business, journalism, the military and the academy discussing political philosophy and public policy. (4) Afternoon and weekend events at places of national and historical interest, to see politics through art, history and military decision making.
Cost and compensation: All students participate free of charge, live in complimentary housing in Washington, DC, and receive a $3,000 stipend. The fellowship is a full-time opportunity, and participants cannot hold other internships or work during the program.
Who should apply: Applicants should be interested in political thought and public policy, be good writers, and want to spend their summer in an intensive academic environment. The program is open to college students and recent graduates.
How to apply: Provide basic contact information and upload a resume or CV; a personal statement of 1,000 words or fewer answering one of two questions (what book has influenced you most and why, or what you hope to gain from the serious study of politics); a writing sample of 15 pages or fewer written solely by you on a related subject such as political science, philosophy, literature, history, classics, policy, foreign affairs or government; a letter of recommendation; and a professional-style headshot. If your school or program does not assign essays, upload documentation explaining that policy plus a 1,000-word answer to the personal statement question you did not choose, written to imitate an academic writing sample. Your recommender receives an automated request when you submit, so ask them well in advance.
Deadlines: The Early Decision deadline is January 9, 2027 at 11:59 p.m. EST, with notification by February 19 and two weeks to decide; accepting an early decision spot is binding, and applicants who are not admitted early decision can be reconsidered in the regular cycle. The Regular Decision deadline is March 16, 2027 at 11:59 p.m. EST. Questions go to Ayla McBreen at amcbreen@hudson.org.
